analysis.one_liner: Eliminates interest on federal student loans and caps future rates based on income.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce and Budget committees on July 27, 2023, received no committee action or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal student lending: starting July 1, 2024, no interest would accrue on existing federal Direct Loans, and older federally backed loans held by private lenders would be refinanced into zero-interest loans. New loans after that date would carry a tiered rate based on the borrower's income — zero for borrowers up to 400% of area median income, and never more than 4%. All loan repayments would flow into an Education Affordability Trust Fund, and any surplus could fund supplemental Pell Grants. The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce and Budget committees and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of current and future student loan borrowers. Existing borrowers would stop paying interest — meaning payments would go entirely to principal, and people would pay off their loans years sooner for thousands of dollars less. Future borrowers would pay 0% interest if their family income is under 400% of the local median, and at most 4% regardless. Borrowers with older privately held federal loans would get refinanced into these zero-interest loans without fees. Low-income students would gain if trust fund surpluses fund supplemental Pell Grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan borrowers, current and future

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Education Department to modify existing Federal Direct Loans so that no interest accrues beginning July 1, 2024, automatically and without action by the borrower.

Refinances older federally backed loans not held by the Department (privately held FFEL and Perkins loans) into zero-interest consolidation loans, with no origination fees, so those borrowers get the same deal.
For new loans, replaces current interest rates with a tiered rate based on the borrower's income and local median income — 0% for most borrowers and capped at 4% even at the top tier.
Raises annual and aggregate borrowing limits and lets excess earnings from a new Education Affordability Trust Fund fund supplemental Pell Grants for low-income students.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would forgo the interest income it currently collects on its roughly $1.6 trillion student loan portfolio, and taxpayers would effectively absorb the cost of issuing and refinancing zero-interest loans. Loan servicers and any private holders of FFEL/Perkins loans would lose the interest revenue on refinanced debt.

drawbacks.text: The bill costs the federal government a major revenue stream: it converts a loan program that currently returns more than it lends (through interest) into a no-interest program, which must be covered by taxpayers or absorbed by the Treasury.

It eliminates the subsidized Stafford loan program and raises annual and aggregate borrowing limits (for example, raising the independent undergraduate aggregate cap from $57,500 to $63,250), so students could take on more principal even as interest stops accruing — meaning total debt could go up for some students.

The new trust fund would invest hundreds of billions of dollars of loan repayments in bonds, an arrangement with investment risk and administrative complexity that the bill addresses with detailed rules but which critics could reasonably call untested at this scale.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete — most federal borrowers would stop seeing their balance grow from interest, and costs would shift from tens of millions of households to the federal government and, indirectly, to lenders and servicers whose business depends on interest. The drawbacks are real: the bill was not scored in the provided record, and eliminating interest on existing loans is expensive for taxpayers; some analysts argue interest subsidizes the loan program's costs and that borrowers at higher-income schools might simply borrow more; and the bill also phases out subsidized Stafford loans and lets students borrow more overall, which could raise total debt loads even as interest disappears. On balance it would have delivered a substantial, verifiable benefit to ordinary borrowers, at a cost concentrated in federal finances and the lending industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House referred the bill to the Education and Workforce Committee and the Budget Committee on the day it was introduced, July 27, 2023.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — was ever recorded on the bill.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025; bills not passed by the end of a Congress are void and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal finances are spared the cost of zero-interest lending, and the student loan servicing and collections industry keeps the interest-based revenue the bill would have ended. Borrowers, who would have stopped accruing interest, are worse off.

for.name: 29 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Swalwell, Porter, Adams, Takano, and Crockett.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, marked up, or reported the bill out of committee after it was referred on July 27, 2023.

against.name: House Budget Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the bill had no Republican support and the Republican-controlled Education and Workforce Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The federal student loan program currently returns more than it costs because of interest; zero-interest loans eliminate that margin, shifting the cost of lending to the Treasury. This is the main reason the bill carries a large price tag.
Interest is a large share of what borrowers repay; removing it shrinks the balances that servicers are paid to collect on. No servicer industry action appears in the record.

The bill does not constrain tuition; it raises borrowing limits (up to $8,250 more per year) and inflation-indexes them, which leaves colleges free to keep raising prices and simply borrowable amounts rise to meet them. Grants for the Postsecondary Student Success Program are conditioned on institutions keeping tuition growth at or under 3% or having a small endowment [S3], a partial check, but the core structure keeps federal dollars flowing through tuition.
